tasks.extracted: An editorial by six alcohol epidemiologists summarizes Fillmore et al. (2006) as finding no significant protection in studies that kept former and occasional drinkers out of the abstainer group, describes Mendelian randomization as resembling a randomized trial more closely than traditional observational studies, and cites a genetic study in which drinkers carrying a variant linked to lower consumption had lower cardiovascular risk (Holmes et al., 2014). In the authors' stated opinion the protective hypothesis is so undermined that the field is due for repositioning; they recommend that burden-of-disease estimates and guidelines assume no protective effect and that guidelines discourage drinking for health reasons. Declaration of interests: none. Its summaries of other studies are second-hand. Editors' observation: three of its authors (Chikritzhs, Stockwell, Naimi) wrote the 2016 review.

tasks.locator: Results › Health risks associated with alcohol consumption, 2nd paragraph; Methods › Systematic review and meta-analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Summary › Findings
tasks.extracted: The minimum of the DALY-weighted curve over all attributable outcomes (the theoretical minimum risk exposure level) was zero standard drinks a day (95% UI 0.0 to 0.8 drinks a day; the abstract prints the interval per week), and the weighted risk rose monotonically with intake; the protective associations for ischaemic heart disease and diabetes in females were offset mainly by cancers. Weights were each outcome's global age-standardised DALY rate per 100,000 in 2016, both sexes; curves were fitted for 0 to 12.5 standard drinks a day; a covariate for former drinkers in the reference group was kept only for ischaemic heart disease, ischaemic stroke and diabetes. In a sensitivity analysis of the weights, the curve changed significantly only where diabetes and ischaemic heart disease made up more than 60% of deaths.

tasks.extracted: Relative risks for 23 outcomes came from 3,992 estimates in 592 prospective and retrospective studies (about 28 million people); exposure from 694 sources; 195 locations, ages 15 to 95 and older. A standard drink is 10 g of ethanol; current drinking is at least one drink in the past 12 months. Uncertainty intervals are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of 1000 draws carrying sampling error and modelling uncertainty from hyper-parameter selection and parameter estimation. The authors list as limitations that drinking patterns were not modelled, unrecorded consumption may be missed, people under 15 were not assessed and outcomes such as dementia were left out. Funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.

tasks.locator: Methods › Estimating dose–response relative risks, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Methods › Estimating TMREL and NDE, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: GBD 2020 re-reviewed the six outcomes with the most alcohol-attributable DALYs with 71 additional studies, dropped lower respiratory infection and used 22 relative-risk curves (five re-fitted, 17 carried over from GBD 2016), relative to non-drinkers and sampled from 0 to 100 g a day. The theoretical minimum risk exposure level (TMREL) and the non-drinker equivalence (NDE, the intake at which the weighted risk again equals a non-drinker's) come from a weighted average of the curves, each cause weighted by its share of DALYs (years of life lost plus years lived with disability) in each region, age, sex and year. Across all regions, ages, sexes and years the 2020 TMREL ranged from 0 (0 to 0) to 1.87 (0.500 to 3.30) standard drinks (10 g) a day; TMREL and NDE varied significantly by age but not by sex or year. Editors' reading of the methods: one curve per cause is applied to every region, so differences between populations come from their mix of diseases.
